Definition: Rearranging equations and solving for an unknown symbol, such as turning stress = F/A into A = F/stress.
Tracking units through a calculation and converting between them; both sides of an equation must have matching dimensions.
Counting only the digits in a number that carry meaningful precision about an engineering value.
Comparing two quantities as a fraction (ratio) or as parts per hundred (percent), such as 5% of a 200 kN load.
Reading values, slopes, and trends off a graph, such as load versus displacement, and checking what the axes and units say.
ReviewNote: Qwen claimed plots predict failure points.

Definition: A body at rest: forces sum to zero and moments sum to zero, so it neither moves nor rotates.
Stress is force per unit area (Pa or MPa); strain is fractional stretch, change in length divided by original length.
How a beam curves and develops tension and compression when loaded; maximum bending stress is M times c divided by I.
Organizing data in rows and columns to automate repetitive engineering calculations for design checks.
A table holds records in rows and variables in columns; a CSV file stores one as plain text with values separated by commas.
Asking an AI chat tool questions in plain language and checking its answers yourself before relying on them.
Published requirements (codes, often adopted into law) and consensus documents (standards) that set minimum safety and performance criteria for designs.
Computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human judgment, such as recognizing images or writing text.
ReviewNote: Qwen conflated AI with machine learning.

Definition: Computer programs that make decisions using explicit if-then logic written by humans rather than learning from examples.
Algorithms that improve at a task by finding patterns in example data instead of following hand-written rules.
The example data a model learns from; its quality, coverage, and bias limit what the model can do.
Statistical regularities a model extracts from training data; they may not match any cause a person can name.
Rules are written by a person and behave predictably; learned patterns come from data, handle messy inputs, but can fail in unwritten ways.
Assigning a number and unit to a physical quantity with an instrument; design decisions rest on these numbers, which are never exact.
Measuring the same quantity several times to see how much readings scatter and to average out random variation.
Finding the difference between the highest and lowest values in a set of experimental data points.
A consistent offset, such as a mis-zeroed scale, that pushes every reading the same way; accuracy is closeness to the true value.
Working out how the uncertainties in input measurements combine to give the uncertainty of a calculated result.
The smallest change a device can detect, limiting the precision of data collected from sensors or gauges.
AI models trained on huge text collections that read and write text in tokens, small chunks of a word (about three-quarters of a word each).
ReviewNote: Qwen omitted what an LLM is.

Definition: A number from 0 (never) to 1 (certain) for how likely an event is; the chance of not-A is 1 minus the chance of A.
How a language model writes: given the text so far, it assigns probabilities to possible next tokens, picks one, and repeats.
ReviewNote: Qwen implied it always picks the most probable word.

Definition: Settings for picking the next token: low temperature favors the top choice (consistent), high temperature adds randomness (varied).
Text instructions given to an AI model that shape the style and content of what it produces.
When an AI states something false or invented, such as a citation or a number, in a fluent, confident tone.
Comparing AI results to a trusted reference to ensure the answer is accurate and grounded in fact.
A data set is a collection of observations, one per row; each property recorded for them is a variable, one per column.
The average value calculated by summing all measurements and dividing by the total count.
Measures of how much data points differ from the average; standard deviation is the square root of variance.
The ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, used to compare variability between different datasets.
The population is everything you want to know about; the sample is the part you actually measured, used to estimate the whole.
Using the scatter of repeated readings, such as their standard deviation, to state how uncertain a measured value is.
An AI system that works toward a goal you give it by choosing and taking steps, such as running tools, with little step-by-step human input.
ReviewNote: Qwen said agents set their own goals.

Definition: The ability of an AI to trigger external software, like a calculator, to get precise results.
The process where an AI breaks a complex goal into a sequence of smaller, logical steps.
A cycle where an AI observes a result, thinks about the next step, and acts until a task is done.
A continuous flow of timestamped readings from a sensor, such as strain or temperature, arriving as the measurement happens.
Comparing a measurement against a set limit to trigger an alert if a value is too high or low.
A description of how often each value, or range of values, occurs in a data set.
A bar graph that shows the frequency of data falling within specific numerical ranges.
A symmetric bell-shaped distribution with most values near the mean and few far away; described by its mean and standard deviation.
A lopsided distribution with a long tail on one side, so the mean and the median differ.
ReviewNote: Qwen's wording was vague about the tail.

Definition: Data points far from the rest; they may be mistakes or real events, so investigate before deleting them.
Checking each step an AI agent took, including its data, code, and numbers, for mistakes before relying on its conclusion.
Systematic errors in AI output caused by flawed data, leading to incorrect or unfair results.
Errors introduced when the data used to teach an AI does not accurately represent the real world.
A small group that accurately reflects the characteristics of the entire population being studied.
When the data an AI encounters in the real world differs from the data it was trained on.
Applying an AI to a problem or material it was not specifically designed or trained to handle.
A lack of specific scenarios in the training set, leaving the AI unable to handle those cases.
A graph of individual data points plotted on two axes to visualize the relationship between variables.
A number between -1 and 1 describing the strength and direction of a linear relationship between variables.
Finding the best-fit straight line through data points to predict one variable based on another.
A value from 0 to 1 showing how much of the variation in data is explained by a model.
The distinction that two things moving together does not mean one actually causes the other to happen.
A relationship between two variables that looks meaningful but is actually caused by a third factor or random chance.
When an AI presents a wrong answer with high certainty, which can mislead engineers during safety-critical checks.
Reporting a number with more digits than the measuring tool can actually provide, suggesting a precision that doesn't exist.
Using probability and data to support a conclusion instead of relying on a single measurement or a guess.
Selecting a subset of data by chance so every single member has an equal probability of being picked.
The natural difference in results that occurs when different random subsets are taken from the same population.
How much a sample mean is expected to vary from the true mean; estimated as s divided by the square root of n.
The factor, near 2 for large samples and bigger for small ones, that multiplies the standard error to set an interval's width.
A range built from sample data that captures the true mean in a stated share (such as 95%) of repeated samples.
ReviewNote: Qwen's wording implied a probability about one interval.

Definition: How often the interval-building method captures the true value across repeated samples, such as 95% of the time.
A p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if there were no real effect; small values suggest it isn't chance.
ReviewNote: Qwen said it determines whether an effect is real.

Definition: A screen showing key measured numbers (metrics), often as charts, so a system's state can be read at a glance.
A sequence of measurements taken at consistent intervals over time to track changes or trends.
A summary document produced by an AI, requiring human verification to ensure the technical conclusions are sound.
The ability of an AI to make decisions and execute tasks without needing constant human input.
A planned stop in an automated process where a human must verify the AI's work before it continues.
Picking the most effective visual representation to make data relationships easy to understand.
The range, starting value (baseline), and spacing (linear or log) of a graph's axes, which shape how big a trend looks.
Graphs whose scale, baseline, or choice of data leaves the viewer with a false impression, deliberately or not.
Evaluating AI-made visuals for inaccuracies in scale or logic to ensure they don't misrepresent engineering data.
A system of automated steps that moves raw data from a source to a final destination for analysis.
The initial process of pulling raw data from sensors or files into a software system.
Errors when values in different units (meters versus feet) or formats (date styles, decimal commas) are mixed as if they matched.
The process of fixing or removing incorrect, duplicate, or irrelevant data before analyzing it.
Gaps or incorrect entries in a dataset that can lead to wrong conclusions if not properly addressed.
How a mistake made early in a pipeline is carried into every later step and can grow into a large error in the result.
Named containers for data, classified by types such as whole numbers, decimals, or text strings.
A function is a named, reusable block of code; an import loads a library of ready-made functions into your program.
A conditional (if/else) picks which code runs based on a test; a loop repeats code for each item or until a test fails.
Reading a program's error message, starting from the last line, to find what failed and where.
How an AI predicts code by identifying patterns from millions of existing software examples.
Code that looks professional and logical but contains hidden errors that can cause engineering failures.
A plain-text file of Python instructions that a computer runs from top to bottom, such as to automate a calculation.
Writing a detailed request to an AI to generate a specific piece of software.
Executing a set of saved instructions through a computer program to produce a final result.
Building software by describing the desired outcome to an AI, often without reading the code it produces.
A detailed description of a program's requirements written in normal English to guide an AI.
The cycle of requesting code, testing it for errors, and refining the prompt until it works.
A specific set of inputs and the expected result used to verify a program's accuracy.
Reading code an AI wrote to check that it does what you asked, uses the right formulas and units, and hides no mistakes.
ReviewNote: Qwen narrowed it to physics laws.

Definition: AI software that can write, execute, and fix its own code to solve a technical problem autonomously.
Small automated checks and the software used to run them to verify that a program works correctly.
Automated verification checks created by an AI to test if its own generated code is correct.
An exact mathematical answer derived from formulas, used to verify that a computer's approximation is accurate.
The small, acceptable difference between a calculated value and the true value, often written as a small decimal.

ConceptLabel: Tests Written by the Same AI
Definition: Verification checks created by the same model that wrote the code, which may repeat the same logic errors.
Comparing a computer's result to a value already proven correct in a textbook or industry standard.
Manually solving a simplified version of a problem to ensure a program's logic is sound.
Confirming that a result comes out in the right units and dimensions, such as newtons for force or pascals for stress.
Quickly checking that a result is the right size, within about a factor of ten, to catch large errors.
Testing a program with extreme or unusual inputs to see if the software crashes or fails.
Finding the reason why two different calculation methods produced different results for the same problem.
A flaw in a computer program that causes it to produce an incorrect or unexpected result.
The process of identifying and fixing errors in a computer program.
Breaking a complex process into smaller parts to find exactly where a mistake is happening.
A sequence of tasks where an AI passes the output of one step as the input for the next.
Reviewing the sequence of an AI's decisions to find where its logic went wrong.
When a small error in an early step of an automated process creates a larger error in later steps.
Using an AI assistant to explain error messages and suggest fixes for broken code.
Providing an AI with the specific error message and the current code to help it find a solution.
The difference between the fundamental flaw causing a bug and the visible error it produces.
Running a program again after a change to ensure the bug is gone and no new errors were added.
Defining the specific limits and intended uses of a software tool to prevent it from being used incorrectly.
A repetitive cycle of prototyping, testing, and refining a design until it meets all requirements.
Ensuring a structure works under various conditions, such as maximum wind, snow, and seismic loads.
Running a calculation or simulation many times while varying one or more inputs to see how they affect the result.
ReviewNote: Qwen limited it to a single input.

Definition: When repeated design adjustments lead to a stable solution that no longer changes significantly.
When an AI slowly deviates from the original project specifications during a long, multi-step process.
Software used to perform complex math, such as beam analysis, to speed up the design process.
The data entered into a system and the results it produces based on those entries.
Checking that data entered into a program is within realistic physical limits before processing it.
A written record of the assumptions and simplifications behind a design, such as loads and material values, so others can check the logic.
Comparing a software's result to a known correct answer from a textbook or lab test.
AI that finds and summarizes technical information faster than manual searching; its sources and claims still need checking.
A condensed version of research papers that highlights the key findings relevant to a project.
Checking that a quoted fact actually exists in the original source and is attributed correctly.
Balancing competing goals, such as reducing cost while increasing structural strength.
Using AI to quickly compare different design options to find the best balance of competing goals.
Using professional experience and physics knowledge to decide if a result is reasonable, regardless of what a tool says.
Assessing the probability of a failure and the potential harm it could cause to people or the environment.
The specific way in which a component or system fails to perform its intended function.
Software that makes and executes decisions without human intervention, posing unique safety and legal challenges.
A requirement that a qualified person must review and approve an AI's decision before implementation.
The principle that the licensed engineer, not the software, answers for a design's safety; exact legal liability depends on the situation.
The study of how to use AI responsibly, focusing on safety, fairness, and transparency.
How well a person can understand and describe why an AI produced a given result; for many models this is only partial.
Checking the final work of an AI to ensure it is technically sound and meets all specifications.
Checking that a design meets the adopted building codes and standards that apply to it.
ReviewNote: Here 'code' means building code, not software.

Definition: Having a second, unrelated person or team check calculations to catch overlooked errors.
A standardized list of checks to ensure every part of a design has been reviewed and validated.
Keeping a written record of every verification step to provide evidence that a design is safe.
A system where a failure could result in serious injury, loss of life, or significant environmental damage.
A state license to offer engineering services to the public; the PE stamp shows a licensed engineer did or directly supervised the work.
ReviewNote: Qwen overstated it as full legal responsibility. Rules vary by state.

Definition: Direct control and personal supervision of engineering work by a licensed engineer, who cannot simply sign off on work others did.
The practice of using AI to help document work while maintaining that the human engineer is ultimately responsible.
Stating when and how AI was used in a project so reviewers, clients, and regulators know what to check.
What AI cannot be relied on to do, such as guarantee correctness, apply physics it was not shown, or handle new situations.
ReviewNote: Qwen made a contested claim about 'truly understanding'.

Definition: Situations where AI fails to identify possible failure modes or ignores the building codes that apply.
Situations that are so unusual they were not part of the AI's training data, making its predictions unreliable.
Know-how engineers gain from experience that is hard to write down, plus physical understanding that AI pattern-matching may lack.
ReviewNote: Qwen omitted what tacit knowledge means.

Definition: Using professional experience to spot and correct AI mistakes that look plausible but violate physical laws.
Deciding against using AI when the risk of error is too high or when a precise, verifiable manual calculation is required.
Evaluating how AI influenced a design process to improve future reliability and maintain professional standards.
